title: Streaming cascade: throttle amplification, partial-token duplication, and idempotency playbook
creator: Ava Patel
description:
Summary:
On 2026-02-26 during a sustained high-concurrency traffic spike we observed a cascading degradation in our streaming paths that manifested as client disconnects, truncated/duplicated token fragments on reconnect, and elevated tail latency for affected sessions. This ticket tracks the post-incident analysis and the set of mitigations (short-, medium-, and long-term) required to prevent repeat events.

Impact:
- ~12% of active streaming sessions across the US-west region experienced at least one disconnect during the 18:42-19:10 UTC window.
- Of disconnected sessions, ~9% reported partial or duplicate token fragments on client-side reassembly (SDK telemetry).
- Several paying customers reported degraded UX; we issued credits and customer notifications via CS.

Timeline (abridged):
- 18:36 UTC: Traffic ramp from a large customer test started.
- 18:42 UTC: First spike in per-worker in-flight requests; scheduler latencies increased.
- 18:45 UTC: Some stream handlers hit the adaptive-batching buffer limit and began delaying backpressure signals to upstream fanout.
- 18:48 UTC: Upstream fanout continued to forward tokens without receiving timely backpressure; overall token throughput increased, causing CPU scheduling stalls and increased socket write latency.
- 18:52 UTC: Connection timeouts increased; clients attempted reconnects. Reconnect flow lacked a monotonic fragment sequence check, resulting in duplicated partial-token fragments for some SDK versions.
- 19:10 UTC: Traffic subsided; we scaled additional pool capacity and the platform recovered.

Root cause (summary):
1) Regression in adaptive-batching layer (a performance micro-optimization landed two weeks prior) changed the semantics of the per-session backpressure window. Under extreme concurrency this modification delayed explicit backpressure propagation to upstream routers, allowing request fanout to exceed capacity.
2) Scheduler and kernel-selection thrashing under transient overload caused CPU stalls that amplified write latency to streaming sockets.
3) Reconnect flow in several SDK versions did not enforce idempotent fragment reassembly (no monotonic fragment sequence or global session generation id), so retries sometimes reintroduced fragments that had already been partially received by the client.
4) Insufficient circuit-breaker thresholds and no per-session admission control to limit short-lived burst fanout from a single client.

Contributing/observability gaps:
- We lacked a high-cardinality metric correlating per-session backpressure delay and downstream queue buildup.
- Existing alerts only flagged worker CPU and global queue depth; there was no rapid alert for "backpressure not signaled for Xs".
- SDKs lacked an instrumentation flag that emits fragment-sequence mismatches during reconnection attempts.

Short-term mitigations (0-7 days):
- Revert the adaptive-batching micro-optimization in prod for US-west traffic while we validate a safe patch (owner: Diego Martinez, PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4891). Target rollout: canary today, full rollback within 3 hours if stability improves.
- Deploy an emergency runbook step: when worker backpressure exceeds 250ms for >30s, proactively reject new fanout and return 429 with retry-after for non-SLA customers (owner: SRE team, runbook PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runbooks/pull/77).
- Patch SDKs (v1.12.4-hotfix) to add a lightweight idempotency token header on streaming start and to log fragment sequence numbers to telemetry so we can detect mismatch rates (owner: SDK lead, PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-js/pull/212).

Medium-term mitigations (1-6 weeks):
- Introduce per-session sequence numbers for fragments and require servers to discard fragments older or equal to the last-acknowledged sequence for that session. Server change owner: Diego Martinez (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4927).
- Implement a per-client short-term admission controller that limits burst fanout (default cap 20 concurrent streams per client token); make cap configurable per-customer (owner: infra-serving, issue: ENG-96210).
- Add a high-cardinality metric and alert: "backpressure_signal_delay_ms" tagged by worker_id and session_id with a P0 alert if median > 300ms for 60s. Dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.example/d/streaming/backpressure-signals.

Long-term mitigations (6+ weeks):
- Rework adaptive-batching state machine to be explicit about backpressure propagation guarantees under overload; add formal unit tests and chaos tests that simulate fanout storms (owner: serving runtime team).
- Add server-side fragment checkpointing so reconnects can resume from the last committed token offset rather than naive replays.
- Implement automated traffic shaping per-route based on real-time queue occupancy and cost SLOs (integrate with Smart Routing policy engine).

Testing & validation plan:
- New load tests reproducing the incident pattern: 10k concurrent connections, controlled burst fanout, varying KV cache hit ratios. Test harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/load-tests/tree/streaming-cascade.
- Staged rollout plan: canary -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with automated rollback if disconnect rate exceeds 0.5% above baseline in 10 minutes.

Customer communication:
- CS already issued credits to the affected customers and provided incident summary. We'll follow up with an engineering summary and the planned fixes in the next customer update.

Acceptance criteria before close:
- Reversion and SDK hotfix deployed to prod and verified in US-west with disconnect rate back to baseline.
- New backpressure metric and alert firing in staging and prod.
- Server fragment sequence enforcement implemented and validated in staging with SDKs honoring idempotency tokens.

Notes:
- This ticket focuses on cross-cutting guardrails (backpressure amplification and idempotency). Separate follow-ups will track the deeper runtime rewrite work (design RFC required).
